meta.notes: Original NMAT-style practice items. These are not actual or reconstructed NMAT questions. The set uses the three Perceptual Acuity item types documented by CEM: Hidden Figure, Mirror Image, and Identical Information. Practice distribution: 10 items per type. Answer keys are distributed across A-E to avoid a predictable pattern.
validationNotes: Hidden Figure uses a simple target plus five complicated drawings.
Mirror Image uses one asymmetric figure plus five visual options.
Identical Information uses a sentence, biographical entry, or bibliographical entry and tests exact matching of spelling, punctuation, and word sequence.

The official NMAT documentation identifies 40 Perceptual Acuity items with a 40-minute recommended time allotment in the published NMAT bulletin; this 30-item set is a practice set, not an official simulation length.

questions.prompt: Which complicated drawing contains the simple target figure?
questions.explanation: The target figure -- a four-sided shape with a flat top edge, a short diagonal edge down to a sharp right-pointing vertex, a long diagonal edge down to a sharp bottom vertex, and a concave arc closing it back to the top-left corner -- is embedded in Drawing C near the upper-center of the circle. It appears in essentially the same orientation as the simple figure, merely shifted to a different position within the circle, with its exact proportions preserved. The other drawings contain similarly styled lines and curves, but none reproduces the target's specific vertex angles, edge lengths, and arc curvature together as a single closed region.
questions.hint: Lock onto the one curved (concave) edge of the target and the sharp point directly opposite it -- this pairing is the most distinctive feature to scan for inside each circle, since most distractor lines in this item are straight.

questions.prompt: Which complicated drawing contains the simple target figure?
questions.explanation: The target figure -- an elongated, boot-shaped outline with several gently bending straight edges along its left side, a short notch near the top, a sharp inner vertex, a pointed lower-right corner, and a small curved (hooked) edge near its opposite end -- is traced by the leftmost diagonal, the near-vertical line, and the small curved hook inside Drawing A, rotated roughly 155-160 degrees from its original orientation. Every edge of the target lines up with an actual drawn line in Drawing A, including the distinctive curved hook near the bottom. In Drawings B, C, D, and E, at least part of the same outline either falls on blank space or only appears to match by tracing the diamond-and-circle frame that is common to all five drawings, rather than the unique lines specific to that option.
questions.hint: All five drawings share the same outer hourglass-and-diamond frame, so ignore that outline entirely -- it's common to every option and can't help you. Focus only on the internal lines unique to each drawing, and look for the one small curved (hooked) segment paired with a long, gently bending straight edge running most of the figure's length.

Search each drawing for a slender, dagger-like cluster of lines near the rim of the circle, then check whether that same small step-in appears at the matching spot before locking in your answer.

questions.prompt: Which option is the correct mirror image of the given figure?
questions.explanation: The target figure is a 3D rectangular prism (drawn with solid visible edges and dashed hidden edges) marked with a horizontal line, a near-vertical box edge, a shorter vertical mark stroke, and a diagonal stroke running from lower-left to upper-right through the center. In the correct mirror image, the entire figure reverses left-to-right: the diagonal stroke now runs from upper-left to lower-right, and the paired vertical lines (the box's near edge and the mark's own vertical stroke) shift to the left side of the dashed hidden edge instead of the right side, as they appear in the original. Option A reproduces this reversal correctly. Option B keeps the same left-of-dashed placement but does not reduce one of the paired vertical strokes to the shorter length seen in a true mirror. Option C introduces an extra hidden (dashed) edge that does not exist in the original figure. Option D shortens the mark's vertical stroke incorrectly, cutting off its upward portion instead of preserving a stroke that extends both above and below the crossing point. Option E reverses the vertical pair's placement correctly but reduces the diagonal to a partial ray instead of a full line running through the center.
questions.hint: Focus on two things: which side of the dashed hidden edge the pair of close vertical lines falls on, and which way the diagonal stroke tilts. A true mirror image reverses both of these from the original — it does not simply rotate the figure or leave the internal lines unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which option is the correct mirror image of the given figure?
questions.explanation: Option A is the correct mirror image. When the figure is reflected across a vertical mirror axis, its left and right sides are reversed while its shape, size, and relative positions of the internal lines remain unchanged. In the original figure, the distinctive diagonal divisions on the left and right lobes have specific orientations. After reflection, these diagonal lines switch sides and reverse their left-to-right direction. Option A reproduces these relationships correctly. The other options alter one or more internal line positions or orientations rather than producing a complete left-to-right reflection.
questions.hint: Focus on the internal diagonal lines in the two side lobes. A vertical mirror swaps the left and right sides and reverses the direction of each diagonal, while keeping the overall shape and size the same.

questions.prompt: Which option is the correct mirror image of the given figure?
questions.explanation: Option D is the correct mirror image because every part of the original square is reversed from left to right while keeping the same size and vertical position. The large circular shape with the square-shaped cutout in the upper-left of the original moves to the upper-right, with the cutout now appearing at the upper-right corner. Likewise, the polygon containing a circle in the upper-right moves to the upper-left, with its slanted sides reversed. In the lower half, the simple triangle that was in the lower-left moves to the lower-right, while the more complex triangular shape with the smaller polygon inside it moves from the lower-right to the lower-left. Option D preserves these four major positions and correctly reverses the internal shapes and line orientations. The other options have one or more details that remain in their original orientation or are altered rather than fully reflected.
questions.hint: Divide the figure into four sections and check them one at a time. The upper-left circle moves to the upper-right, the upper-right polygon moves to the upper-left, and the two lower shapes also switch sides. Check the small cutouts and internal lines to make sure they are reversed, not simply moved.

questions.prompt: Which option is the correct mirror image of the given figure?
questions.explanation: The target figure is a rose bloom with a curling stem and leaf fronds below it. In the correct mirror image, the entire figure reverses left-to-right: the upward-pointing inner petal leans the opposite direction, the petal folds and overlaps swap sides, and the stem's curl and the leaf fronds beneath it curve the opposite way, with the stem's cut tip ending on the mirrored side. Option E reproduces this reversal correctly across the bloom, the petal overlaps, and the stem/frond curvature. Options A, B, C, and D retain at least one element of the original figure's orientation instead of reversing it fully, making them distractors that mirror only part of the figure or preserve the original's curl direction.
questions.hint: Don't just check the rose bloom at the top — it can look deceptively similar across options. Trace the stem down to its curling tip and check which way it bends, and which way the leaf fronds point. A true mirror reverses the curl direction of the stem and fronds, not just the general outline.

questions.prompt: Which option is the correct mirror image of the given figure?
questions.explanation: The target figure, enclosed in a square frame, shows a hexagon on the left overlapping a tilted rectangle, which in turn overlaps a circle topped by a downward-pointing triangle on the right. In the correct mirror image, the entire arrangement reverses left-to-right: the triangle-and-circle cluster moves to the left side of the frame and the hexagon moves to the right side, with the tilted rectangle's overlap pattern reversing to match. Option A reproduces this correctly, placing the triangle and circle on the left and the hexagon on the right. The other options either keep the hexagon on the left (failing to reverse the overall layout) or alter the overlap relationships between the shapes instead of simply mirroring their positions.
questions.hint: Ignore the individual shapes' own symmetry (the circle and triangle look the same either way) and focus on which side of the frame the hexagon ends up on versus the triangle-and-circle cluster. A true mirror swaps their left-right positions entirely.

questions.prompt: Which option is the correct mirror image of the given figure?
questions.explanation: The target figure shows two hanging bean pods with a veined leaf and a small curling tendril positioned at the upper-left, overlapping the left pod. In the correct mirror image, the entire figure reverses left-to-right: the leaf and tendril move to the upper-right, overlapping the right pod instead, while the two pods themselves keep their bumpy internal seam pattern but in mirrored left-right order. Option C reproduces this correctly, with the leaf and tendril shifted to the right side. The other options either leave the leaf on the left (matching the original instead of its mirror) or place it in a way that doesn't consistently reverse its position and overlap with the pods.
questions.hint: Focus on the leaf and the small curling tendril near the top of the pods rather than the pods themselves, since the pods look similar either way. A true mirror moves the leaf from the upper-left to the upper-right side of the figure.

questions.prompt: Which option is the correct mirror image of the given figure?
questions.explanation: The target figure is a pinwheel-like cross shape: a square outline with a notch cut into each of its four corners, all offset in the same rotational direction, which gives the whole figure a chirality (it cannot be rotated to match its own reflection). In the correct mirror image, this rotational offset reverses direction entirely — every notch that was cut toward one rotational sense now cuts toward the opposite sense, flipping the pinwheel's apparent spin. Option A reproduces this correctly, with the notch pattern reversed at every corner. The other options either preserve the original figure's rotational direction (making them identical or rotated versions of the original rather than true mirrors) or reverse the notches inconsistently at only some corners.
questions.hint: Ignore the overall square outline, since it looks the same either way. Instead, pick one corner notch and trace which direction it 'cuts' relative to the edges around it — a true mirror reverses this cutting direction at every corner, giving the whole shape the opposite rotational spin.

questions.prompt: Which option is the correct mirror image of the given figure?
questions.explanation: The target figure is a mushroom whose cap has unevenly spaced gill lines (denser and more angled toward one side) and whose stem curves out to one side before curving back at the base, both of which break the figure's left-right symmetry. In the correct mirror image, both of these asymmetric features reverse together: the denser cluster of gill lines shifts to the opposite side of the cap, and the stem's curve bows out in the opposite direction. Option B reproduces this correctly, with the gill pattern and stem curvature both reversed from the original. The other options either mirror only one of these two features, or preserve the stem's original curve direction while only adjusting the cap, producing an inconsistent transformation rather than a true mirror.
questions.hint: Don't just check the cap outline, since mushroom caps look similar either way. Trace the stem's curve from top to bottom and compare it with how the gill lines bunch together on one side of the cap — a true mirror reverses both of these together, not just one.

questions.prompt: Which option is the correct mirror image of the given figure?
questions.explanation: The target figure is a rectangle divided by five vertical lines (including its two side edges), where some lines are solid and others are dashed with gaps at specific heights. This solid/dashed sequence, read left to right, is not symmetric. In the correct mirror image, the entire left-to-right sequence of solid and dashed lines reverses: a line that was solid on the original's left side becomes dashed on the mirror's right side, and vice versa, with each dash's gap position also reversing in left-right order. Option B reproduces this correctly, with the dashed lines and their gap positions appearing in reversed order compared to the original. The other options either keep the original's solid/dashed sequence unchanged or reverse only part of the pattern.
questions.hint: Ignore the outer rectangle outline and instead read the sequence of internal lines from left to right, noting which are solid and which are dashed. A true mirror image reverses this entire left-to-right sequence, not just one or two lines.

questions.prompt: Which option is the correct mirror image of the given figure?
questions.explanation: The target figure shows four screw-head circles woven together by interlocking rounded bands, arranged so the top-left circle has a vertical double-slot head, the top-right circle has a single horizontal slot, and the two bottom circles have diagonal slots tilted in opposite directions. In the correct mirror image, the entire arrangement reverses left-to-right: the horizontal-slot circle moves to the top-left, the vertical double-slot circle moves to the top-right, the two diagonal-slot circles swap corners, and each diagonal slot's tilt direction reverses to match its new position. Option D reproduces this correctly. The other options either leave the horizontal- and vertical-slot circles in their original left-right positions, or move the circles without correctly reversing the diagonal slots' tilt direction.
questions.hint: Check two things together: which corner each screw-slot style (vertical, horizontal, or diagonal) ends up in, and which way the diagonal slots tilt. A true mirror image swaps left and right corners and also flips the tilt direction of the diagonal slots — moving the circles alone isn't enough.

questions.prompt: Which option is the correct mirror image of the given figure?
questions.explanation: The target figure is an eye and eyebrow drawn with clear left-right asymmetry: the eyebrow tapers from a thicker, curled end on the left to a thin point on the right; the eye's rounded tear-duct (inner corner) sits on the left; and the bold cluster of upper lashes, along with the small lower lash marks, sits at the outer corner on the right. In the correct mirror image, all three features reverse together: the eyebrow's thick end moves to the right, the tear-duct moves to the right side of the eye, and the lash cluster moves to the left side. Option E reproduces this correctly, with the eyebrow taper, tear-duct position, and lash cluster all consistently reversed. The other options reverse only some of these features while leaving others in their original position, producing an inconsistent, non-mirrored figure.
questions.hint: Check three things together, not just one: which end of the eyebrow is thicker, which corner of the eye has the rounded tear-duct shape, and which corner has the bold lash cluster. A true mirror reverses all three in the same direction — mirroring only the eyebrow or only the lashes is a common trap.

questions.prompt: Which option is the correct mirror image of the given figure?
questions.explanation: The target figure is a 3D polyhedron (gem-like solid) drawn in wireframe, with a diamond-shaped central face and an asymmetric arrangement of surrounding facets: a narrower cluster of facets meeting at a sharp vertex on the upper-left, and a wider facet extending outward to a point on the right. In the correct mirror image, this facet arrangement reverses left-to-right: the narrow, sharply-angled cluster moves to the upper-right, and the wider extending facet moves to the left, while the central diamond face's orientation reverses to match. Option D reproduces this correctly. The other options either preserve the original's facet arrangement on the same side or distort the central diamond face's proportions instead of simply mirroring it.
questions.hint: Focus on the central diamond-shaped face and the sharp vertex point nearest it, rather than the overall outline (which can look similar across options). A true mirror moves the sharp vertex and its narrow facet cluster to the opposite side of the figure.

questions.prompt: Which option is the correct mirror image of the given figure?
questions.explanation: The target figure is a striped half-dome with its flat edge on the right, a large triangle attached to its left (rounded) side pointing outward to the left, and a small circle attached to its flat right edge containing a tiny triangle pointing inward toward the dome.
